title: Year two opens: a library, not a book
hookLine: the Catholic Bible has 73 books; Protestant Bibles have 66, and Orthodox Bibles a few more

lines: AN ORTHODOX BIBLE: A FEW MORE.
cards: Pick up a Bible from a Catholic parish and count the contents page: seventy-three. Borrow one from the Baptist church down the road and count again: sixty-six. An Orthodox friend's runs a few books longer still.
Same Genesis at the front. Same Gospels. Same Revelation, or Apocalypse, at the back.
And yet the number on the shelf is different. Most people never notice, because nobody counts a contents page. Year two reads the Bible in order, from its first line, so first, a look at the shelf.

teach.b: Bible comes from the Greek ta biblia: the books. Plural. It's a library, written across many centuries in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek, holding poems, laws, letters, family stories, prophecy and prayer.
The list has a name: canon.

In Greek, kanon was a measuring rod, a straight reed builders used to check a line. It came to mean a rule, and then the list of books the Church receives as scripture, the measure it reads everything else by.
The Catholic list has forty-six books in the Old Testament and twenty-seven in the New: seventy-three.
Early councils at Hippo and Carthage, around the year four hundred, gave lists like this, and the Council of Trent defined it in fifteen forty-six.
Seven of those Old Testament books, Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and the two books of Maccabees, plus longer forms of Esther and Daniel, came down to the early Church in Greek.
Catholics call them deuterocanonical, the second canon.
Protestant churches follow the shorter Hebrew list for the Old Testament; many older Protestant Bibles, the 1611 King James among them, printed those books in a middle section called the Apocrypha.
Orthodox churches keep them and a few more, and their lists vary. Each church reads its own shelf faithfully.
And why it matters on an ordinary Tuesday: open this library and you're not reading one author's opinion. You're walking into a room where many voices, across many centuries, talk about the same God.

how: Catholic Bibles print seventy-three books, including Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and 1 and 2 Maccabees, and the deuterocanonical books are read at Mass through the Church's year like any other part of scripture.

games.q: you're a bishop at the Council of Trent in 1546. the Church is divided, and people are asking which books belong in the Bible. what does the council do?
o: leave every church to decide for itself.
name the list of books the Church receives, seventy-three in all.
leave the question for a later council.
games.why: Trent defined the canon: forty-six Old Testament books and twenty-seven New, matching the lists earlier councils like Hippo and Carthage had given.

practice: Open your Bible to the contents page, or if you don't have one, picture a long shelf.

Run your finger down the list slowly, one name at a time, the way you'd read names on a memorial: the ones you know, the ones you've never heard of, and where the shelf changes, from the books of Moses to the histories, the poems, the prophets, then the Gospels and the letters.
You don't need to finish; if you pray, ask for a good year of reading.
